name: Natto
teaser: Fermented soybeans bound in a web of sticky strings — a Japanese breakfast staple with a smell some love and many fear. The fermentation is done by Bacillus subtilis, which produces the strings and a deep, umami funk.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how natto is made by steaming soybeans and fermenting them with Bacillus subtilis. Write how the stirring develops its strings, what makes its flavor, and why it is praised for its health benefits.

name: Umami
teaser: The 'fifth taste' — savory, brothy, meaty — discovered by Japanese chemist Kikunae Ikeda in 1908, who isolated glutamate from seaweed broth. Your tongue has receptors for it, and it is why tomatoes, aged cheese, and soy sauce are irresistible.

exploreAction.targetName: Umami foods and the science of taste
exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Ikeda discovered umami in kombu broth and how the taste works through glutamate receptors. Write a list of umami-rich foods you can find, and how chefs combine them to deepen flavor.

name: Kombucha
teaser: A fizzy fermented tea, alive with a rubbery culture called a SCOBY — a community of yeast and bacteria. It has been brewed for centuries, possibly in ancient China, and every batch grows a new SCOBY like a living heirloom.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how a SCOBY ferments sweet tea into tangy, fizzy kombucha over a week or two. Write the roles of yeast and bacteria, why a pellicle forms on top, and how flavors are added in a second fermentation.

name: Miso
teaser: A fermented soybean paste aged in cedar barrels for months or years — the soul of Japanese soup. Its flavor deepens with age, and a good miso maker tends their barrels like a sommelier tends wine.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how miso is made from soybeans, koji (rice inoculated with mold), and salt, then aged. Write how the aging time changes color and flavor from white to red, and how miso is used beyond soup.

name: Yakitori
teaser: Skewered chicken grilled over binchotan — a white-hot charcoal made from oak that burns clean and evenly — with nothing but salt or tare sauce. In Japan, a yakitori master may cook one cut for decades before perfecting it.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn what binchotan charcoal is and why it grills so evenly. Write about the cuts of yakitori from thigh to skin, the role of tare sauce, and why the skewers are turned with such care.

name: Charcuterie
teaser: The art of preserving and curing meat — from prosciutto hung in mountain air to pâtés and terrines — born of a time before refrigeration. It turns humble pork into works of craft, geography, and patience.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how salami, prosciutto, and other cured meats are made and how salt, fermentation, and drying preserve them. Write the difference between cured and fermented sausage, and how local climates shape each region's charcuterie.

name: Paella
teaser: A saffron-tinted rice dish cooked in a wide, shallow pan over open fire in Valencia — originally a farmer's meal of rice, rabbit, and snails. The socarrat, the caramelized crust at the bottom, is the prize of the pan.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn the traditional Valencian paella method — toast the rice, add broth, and let it cook without stirring until a crust forms. Write what socarrat is, why the pan must be wide, and how seafood paella differs from the original.

name: Tagine
teaser: A conical clay pot that braises slowly, capturing steam and letting it drip back down — a low-fuel, low-water way to cook in the desert. In Morocco, the tagine is both the pot and the slow-cooked stew within it.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how the tagine's cone shape condenses steam and returns moisture to the dish, requiring little water. Write about the classic combinations — lamb with apricots, chicken with preserved lemon — and how it is eaten from the pot.

name: Mole Poblano
teaser: Mexico's most complex sauce — a dark, velvety blend of dozens of ingredients: chiles, chocolate, nuts, seeds, spices, and stale bread — simmered for hours. Legend says a convent invented it for a visiting archbishop.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how mole poblano layers dried chiles, chocolate, nuts, and spices, and why the sauce must simmer long to marry its flavors. Write the legend of its invention and why every mole family recipe is a guarded secret.

name: Tamales
teaser: Masa steamed in corn husks or banana leaves — a Mesoamerican dish so old it appears in Aztec codexes, and so communal that making them is a party called a tamalada. Every region wraps a different filling and a different leaf.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how tamales are made — nixtamalized corn masa, fillings, wrapping, and steaming — and how the tamalada tradition brings families together. Write how tamales differ from Mexico to Guatemala to Venezuela.

name: Sourdough
teaser: Bread leavened not by commercial yeast but by a living culture of wild yeast and bacteria — some starters are kept alive for decades, passed down like family heirlooms. Each culture gives its bread a distinct tang and character.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how a sourdough starter is fed flour and water daily to keep its wild yeast and lactobacilli alive. Write what creates the sour tang, why the dough rises slowly, and how long a well-kept starter can live.

name: Ramen
teaser: A bowl of wheat noodles in rich broth — tonkotsu simmered for days until milky, or shoyu clear and sharp — born from Chinese noodle soups and perfected in Japan. Each bowl is a geography of broths, noodles, and toppings.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn the four main ramen broths — tonkotsu, shoyu, shio, and miso — and how each region specializes. Write what makes noodles springy (kansui), why ramen is eaten fast, and how the dish came to Japan from China.

name: Dim Sum
teaser: A Cantonese brunch of small dishes wheeled past your table on carts — har gow, siu mai, bao, and a hundred more — shared with tea and chatter. It began along the Silk Road as teahouse snacks for travelers.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn the classic dim sum dishes and how the tradition of yum cha (drinking tea) pairs with small plates. Write what har gow and siu mai are made of, and how the cart tradition works at a busy teahouse.

name: Cacao and Chocolate
teaser: Before it was candy, cacao was a Mesoamerican drink so valued that the Aztecs used beans as money and served it frothed with chili. Fermenting, roasting, and grinding the bean is a craft older than Europe's first taste of it.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how cacao pods are fermented, dried, roasted, and ground into chocolate. Write how the Aztecs and Maya used cacao, why beans were currency, and how modern chocolate is made from the same bean.

name: Honey and Bees
teaser: Honey never spoils — sealed pots of it found in Egyptian tombs are still edible after 3,000 years. A single bee makes a twelfth of a teaspoon in its life, and the hive's waggle dance tells sisters exactly where the flowers are.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how bees turn nectar into honey — by adding enzymes and evaporating water until it is too dry for microbes. Write why honey lasts forever, how the waggle dance works, and what makes different floral honeys taste different.

name: Maple Syrup
teaser: Forty liters of maple sap boil down to one liter of syrup — a spring ritual in cold northern forests where trees wake up and push sweet sap through their trunks. Sugar maples, tapped by hand, give their gift for over a century.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how the freeze-thaw cycle of early spring makes sap flow, and how it is collected and boiled down. Write why it takes so much sap for syrup, how the grade system works, and why maple trees can be tapped for decades.

name: Olive Oil
teaser: Liquid gold pressed from olives — some trees in the Mediterranean are over 2,000 years old and still fruiting. Extra virgin means cold-pressed, unrefined, and full of the polyphenols that make it a health legend.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how olives are harvested and cold-pressed within hours to make extra virgin oil. Write what 'extra virgin' actually means, how to taste olive oil properly, and how ancient trees still produce today.

name: Coffee
teaser: From a goat herder who noticed his goats dancing after eating red berries, coffee spread through Sufi monasteries, Ottoman courts, and European cafés. The bean's flavor depends on altitude, soil, processing, and roast — a world in a cup.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how coffee cherries are processed (washed, natural, honey), roasted, and brewed. Write the legend of Kaldi and the goats, how the drink spread, and why origin and altitude shape the flavor.

name: Chanoyu (Tea Ceremony)
teaser: The Japanese Way of Tea — a choreographed ritual of whisking matcha, folding cloth, and bowing that turns a cup of tea into meditation. It teaches wabi-sabi: finding beauty in simplicity, imperfection, and the present moment.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn the steps of chanoyu — the tea room's entrance, the cleaning of the bowl, whisking matcha, and the guests' ritual appreciation. Write what wabi-sabi means and how the ceremony embodies mindfulness.

name: Hanami
teaser: Japan's cherry blossom viewing — families and friends picnic under pink canopies that last barely a week. The blossoms' brief bloom is a meditation on impermanence: beauty that you must catch while it lasts.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how hanami began with aristocrats in the Heian period and how the cherry forecast tracks blooms across Japan. Write why the blossoms are so short-lived and how the custom reflects the idea of impermanence.

name: Holi
teaser: India's festival of colors — a spring celebration where everyone throws clouds of colored powder, drenches each other with water, and erases the lines of class and caste for a day. It honors the coming of spring and the triumph of good.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn the story behind Holi — the legend of Prahlad and Holika — and how the festival is celebrated across India. Write what the colors symbolize, how the festival begins with a bonfire, and how it is celebrated abroad.

name: Songkran
teaser: Thailand's New Year — the world's largest water fight, where the whole country takes to the streets with water guns, buckets, and elephants spraying passersby. The drenching began as a gentle pouring of water over elders' hands as blessing.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Songkran began as a gentle tradition of pouring scented water as a blessing and became a nationwide water battle. Write how the festival marks the Thai New Year, the role of temples, and what the water symbolizes.

name: Obon
teaser: Japan's festival of the dead — a week when ancestral spirits are said to return home, welcomed with lanterns, dances, and family graveside visits. The festival ends with floating lanterns drifting away on rivers and seas.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn how Obon honors ancestors with bon dances, graveside offerings, and floating lanterns. Write the story of its origin — a disciple who danced with joy at freeing his mother's spirit — and how families welcome the spirits home.

name: Diwali
teaser: The festival of lights — rows of oil lamps, fireworks, sweets, and rangoli patterns drawn at doorways — celebrating light's victory over darkness across India and beyond. For five days, homes glow to welcome fortune and joy.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn the stories behind Diwali — from Rama's return to the goddess Lakshmi — and how each day of the festival is observed. Write what diyas and rangoli represent, and how Diwali is celebrated differently across regions.

name: Día de los Muertos Altars
teaser: Mexican ofrendas — home altars layered with marigolds, candles, sugar skulls, and the favorite foods of the departed — built to welcome spirits home for one night. It is a celebration of memory, not mourning.

exploreAction.instruction: Learn the elements of a traditional ofrenda — the photo, marigolds, candles, water, food — and what each layer and object means. Write why the holiday blends Indigenous and Catholic traditions and how it celebrates memory.
